Since the new rules are making it almost impossible to buy a gun with out being a registered owner, (guns are not registered but the Owners are), maybe you should think about making your own. It is not a expensive as you might think. All you need are three pieces of equipment that can be purchased on ebay dirt cheap.

The first thing you need is a pottery kiln, (you need this for making castings, forgings, and heat treating.) A good used one will go for $300-$500.

The next thing you need is a vertical mill. The Bridgeport 9" X 42" J heads go for about $2400 on ebay. The last thing you need and the most expensive is a good high precision accurate metal lathe, for making, rifling, and turning barrels. These puppies go for anywhere between $2000 to $4000 again on ebay.

Hell I saw a complete a pretty good looking Bolton Combination 12" X 36" Lathe with Milling head for $4000 On ebay. http://www.ebay.com/itm/Bolton-Tools-12-x-36-Metal-Lathe-Mill-Drill-Milling-Combo-New-Machine-T400-281813216003?hash=item419d606b03:g:0rwAAOSwys5WVMsu That might be a bit small for standard length rifle barrels though. (Perfect for hand guns though,)

You then need to use the above equipment to build a 1/2 ton trip hammer for forging metal pieces. These trip hammers use a cam to raise the hammer and gravity to cause it to fall.

Once you have the equipment buy some soft steel (1040 is probably the best) for practice in casting, forging and the cutting of steel parts. Once you have a feel for the working of metal and getting what you want, buy some billets of 4140 or 4150 steel. 4140 for receivers and bolts and 4150 for barrels. You are now set up to make your own guns, or to make some money as a manufacturing jobber, (make small parts and assemblies on contract for a larger manufacturing company) Lots of money to be made out there for a jobber. Companies often put things out on contract as there is such a small production run that it doesn't pay to automate the manufacturing process.

So, you've decided you wish to begin adding to or changing Minecraft's code to make something of your own creation. While I am by no means very good at making more than relatively basic mods myself, I would like to give a few pointers and advice for at least getting your foot in the door of Minecraft modding. Keep in mind that this post is meant to cover the PC edition only, and via the Minecraft Forge API at that. If you would like to mod other platforms the game is written for, I would still highly reccomend you start here, as there are a plethora of relevant guides on the internet, and a lot more of which that should well fit your learning style. In addition to this, there is a lot more support from the PC version's larger community, should you run into an issue you simply cannot find a way to resolve.

**Knowing a fair amount of Java is critical to knowing how to manipulate code well**. You could skip this entire paragraph, and head down to the one that jumps straight into setting up a workspace for modifying the game right now (or rather, linking to guides that detail how to do that). However, the more knowledge you have of Java and, much more importantly, the more experience you have using that knowledge to make things, the easier it will be to find ways of implementing what you want (in theory, anyways). In addition, you will be much better equipped in optimizing your mod's source code later, when it becomes necessary.

* [Codecademy](https://www.codecademy.com/) put together an interactive online classrom for Java recently, as well as a considerably large amount of other languages should you wish to learn them as well. This is a great place to start, and while their lessons on Java (not to be confused with JavaScript) only really cover the basics, it's still (at least in my experience) very helpful and effective at setting a good foundation for expanding upon with other guides. * [TheNewBoston](https://youtu.be/Hl-zzrqQoSE) did a video tutorial series to teach Java a while back. It's actually what I started out with, and while I personally haven't gone through more than about twenty or so of his tutorial videos, it's still definitely worth checking out.

When you feel comfortable with Java, you can begin learning how to work with Forge to add things into Minecraft! For the most basic of things, namely adding in items, you will not need to know too much, though I would still reccomend learning some Java so as to give you a better grasp on what is actually going on when you do things. While a lot of the process for these basic things involves merely sticking values into a function that does most of the heavy lifting for you, as you start to make more advanced things you will naturally have a lot easier of a time if you know how to do such things. Also bear in mind that the process of making a mod can vary quite a bit across major versions of Minecraft, and sometimes even a bit across minor updates. Below is a list of modding tutorials that I (or possibly later, other users as well) would reccomend to get you started:

* [Bedrockminer](http://bedrockminer.jimdo.com/modding-tutorials/) has some very useful tutorials for both Minecraft 1.7 and 1.8 at the time of this post's creation. They are all text-based, but provide useful details and even have information on properties of numerous things from vanilla Minecraft to refer to when creating blocks and items, as well as a few others. * MrCrayfish has made video tutorials on the subject ([For 1.7](https://youtu.be/0ULz-oCUbEg?list=PLy11IosblXIExa6zzhjhYNXeBW9o6FhPU) ; [For 1.8](https://youtu.be/VhOSL7rGb10?list=PLy11IosblXIFDFAT3wz_5Nve05wIVKFSJ)). They mainly refer to more basic mod creation, but I found them helpful. Do note though that his 1.8 tutorials are not quite as extensive. * You can also check out the [list of tutorials from the Minecraft Forum](http://www.minecraftforum.net/forums/mapping-and-modding/mapping-and-modding-tutorials), which I actually just came across, but will likely end up referring to in the future. These tutorials are on a wide range of topics which could prove very useful.

If you make something you'd like to share, I'd reccomend uploading it to [Curse](http://www.curse.com/mc-mods/minecraft). If you want to promote it and potentially get more people to see it, posting a thread about it on the [Mods section of the Minecraft Forum](http://www.minecraftforum.net/forums/mapping-and-modding/minecraft-mods) is one of the best ways to do so. Many users frequent the forum looking for something new, and from my experience, your best alternative to this in terms of potential visibility is to post it on Reddit's /r/FeedTheBeast, though your submission will only stay on the subreddit's frontpage for so long (not to mention that most users here probably want as little to do with Reddit as possible, but I find the subreddit's community to be quite supportive of mods that get posted there). Also, I would personally love to see creations from users of this subverse, so please don't hesitate to post it here!

This all may be a bit of a mess, but I hope it helps! One last thing though: if you have any tutorials that you would like to reccomend, please do so and I will likely add them to the list.

Happy coding, everyone!
